title: Fire Marshal operational permits and inspections for a glass studio (LP-gas, oxygen and other compressed gases, hot work, furnaces and kilns, assembly use)
question: My glass studio in Staunton will run a gas furnace, glory hole, kilns and torches and store propane and oxygen, and the public will come in for classes. Which Fire Marshal permits do I need, what do they cost, and what inspections should I expect?
office: Staunton Fire & Rescue, Fire Marshal's Office (the city's fire official under the Virginia Statewide Fire Prevention Code)
summary: Staunton enforces the Virginia Statewide Fire Prevention Code (SFPC) through its Fire Marshal's Office, which issues operational permits, inspects commercial buildings at least yearly and can require notification before any process that produces conditions hazardous to life or property or before a place of assembly is established. Under the state code the fire official may require operational permits for, among other things, LP-gas storage and use (no exemption for a business), compressed gases above threshold amounts (oxygen above 504 cubic feet, flammable gases such as propane or acetylene above 200 cubic feet, inert gases above 6,000), hot work including fixed-site hot work equipment, cutting and welding, industrial ovens, open flames in assembly or dining areas and places of assembly. Staunton's fee schedule (City Code § 15.25.055, read on eCode360) prices an LP-gas permit at $50 a year, a hazardous materials permit at $50 a year, Class II or IIIA liquid storage above 25 gallons at $50 a year, indoor flame-effects material at $100 per event and tents of 400 to 900 square feet at $25 per event, but lists no compressed gas, hot work, industrial oven, open flame or assembly permit; the city's Fire Prevention Activity Application covers other activities that require a permit. So: apply for the LP-gas permit if you use propane, ask the Fire Marshal (540.332.3720) which other permits the office requires for oxygen and flammable gas cylinders, the furnace and glory hole, torches and public classes, pay the fees, pass the inspection before the permit issues, post the permits on the premises, and keep a fire protection system out-of-service notice and fire watch routine ready.

legal_basis.quote: The Fire Prevention Code shall supersede fire prevention regulations heretofore adopted by local governments or other political subdivisions.

Local governments are hereby empowered to adopt fire prevention regulations that are more restrictive or more extensive in scope than the Fire Prevention Code provided such regulations do not affect the manner of construction, or materials to be used in the erection, alteration, repair, or use of a building or structure

Any local government may enforce the Fire Prevention Code in its entirety or with respect only to those provisions of the Fire Prevention Code relating to open burning, fire lanes, fireworks, and hazardous materials.
The local governing body of any jurisdiction that enforces the Code may establish such procedures or requirements as may be necessary for the administration and enforcement of the Code.
A schedule of such costs shall be adopted by the local governing body in a local ordinance.
Appeals concerning the application of the Code by the local enforcing agency shall first lie to a local board of appeals and then to the State Building Code Technical Review Board.

The fire official may require notification prior to (i) activities involving the handling, storage, or use of substances, materials, or devices regulated by the SFPC; (ii) conducting processes that produce conditions hazardous to life or property; or (iii) establishing a place of assembly.

Operational permits may be required by the fire official as permitted under the SFPC in accordance with Table 107.2, except that the fire official shall require permits for the manufacturing, storage, handling, use, and sale of explosives.
Compressed gas. An operational permit is required for the storage, use, or handling at normal temperature and pressure (NTP) of compressed gases in excess of the amounts listed in this table.

legal_basis.citation: 13VAC5-52-70 (SFPC Table 107.2, Permit Amounts for Compressed Gases: flammable 200 cubic feet; inert and simple asphyxiant 6,000; oxidizing including oxygen 504)
legal_basis.quote: Oxidizing (including oxygen)
Cutting and welding. An operational permit is required to conduct cutting or welding operations within the jurisdiction.
3. Fixed-site hot work equipment such as welding booths.
Industrial ovens. An operational permit is required for operation of industrial ovens regulated by Chapter 30.

Exception: An operational permit is not required for individual containers with a 500-gallon (1893 L) water capacity or less or multiple container systems having an aggregate quantity not exceeding 500 gallons (1893 L), serving occupancies in Group R-3.
Open flames and candles. An operational permit is required to use open flames or candles in connection with assembly areas or dining areas of restaurants or drinking establishments.
Places of assembly. An operational permit is required to operate a place of assembly.
Commercial cooking. An operational permit is required for the operation of commercial cooking appliances in occupancies other than assembly occupancies or dwellings.
Application for a permit shall be made on forms prescribed by the fire official.

Before a permit is issued, the fire official shall make such inspections or tests as are necessary to ensure that the use and activities for which application is made comply with the provisions of this code.
Permits shall remain in effect until revoked or for such period as specified on the permit. Permits are not transferable.
Issued permits shall be kept on the premises designated therein at all times and shall be readily available for inspection by the fire official.

A permit shall become invalid if the authorized activity is not commenced within six months after issuance of the permit or if the authorized activity is suspended or abandoned for a period of six months after the time of commencement.
In accordance with § 27-98 of the Code of Virginia, fees may be levied by the local governing body in order to defray the cost of enforcement and appeals under the SFPC.
A permit shall not be issued until the designated fees have been paid.

steps.step: List the regulated materials and processes in the studio
steps.how: Write down, with quantities: propane (LP-gas) cylinders or tank and their water capacity; oxygen cylinders (cubic feet at normal temperature and pressure); any acetylene, natural gas-fed torches, compressed air or inert gases; the gas-fired furnace, glory hole and kilns and their fuel; torches and other open-flame work; flammable liquids (solvents, polishing compounds) and combustible liquids; the public rooms and how many people will be in them for classes or events; and any sprinkler or alarm system. Compare the list with SFPC Table 107.2: permits may be required for LP-gas storage and use (the exemption for containers of 500 gallons or less applies only to Group R-3 homes), compressed gases above 200 cubic feet of flammable gas, 504 cubic feet of oxygen or 6,000 cubic feet of inert gas, hazardous materials above table amounts, Class I liquids above 5 gallons inside, Class II or IIIA liquids above 25 gallons inside, hot work and fixed-site hot work equipment, cutting and welding, industrial ovens, open flames in assembly or dining areas, places of assembly and commercial cooking.
steps.deadline: Before storing any propane, oxygen or flammable gas on site
steps.quote: Compressed gas. An operational permit is required for the storage, use, or handling at normal temperature and pressure (NTP) of compressed gases in excess of the amounts listed in this table.

steps.step: Call the Fire Marshal's Office early and ask which permits Staunton requires for your list
steps.who: Studio owner; Fire Marshal's Office (540.332.3720, Monday through Friday 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; firemarshals@ci.staunton.va.us)
steps.how: The state code leaves it to each locality to say which Table 107.2 permits it requires and what they cost. Staunton's fee ordinance (§ 15.25.055, read on eCode360) lists LP-gas, hazardous materials, flammable and combustible liquids, explosives and fireworks, flame-effects material, tents, amusement buildings, carnivals and scrap tires, and the city's permit page offers a Fire Prevention Activity Application for other activities that require a permit. Compressed gases, hot work, industrial ovens, open flames and places of assembly are not priced on the local schedule, so whether the office requires a permit for oxygen cylinders, the furnace and glory hole, torches or classes is its call. The fire official may also require advance notification of any process that produces conditions hazardous to life or property and of establishing a place of assembly. Ask at the same time about cylinder storage and separation, furnace clearances, exhaust, extinguishers and exits, so the building plans match what the inspection will look for.
steps.deadline: Before the building permit plans are final, and in any case before gases are delivered
steps.quote: For other activities not listed but require a permit.

steps.step: Apply for the LP-gas (propane) permit and any flammable or combustible liquid permit
steps.how: Use the city's LP Gas or Flammable/Combustible Liquid Storage Permit Application (the PDF has no archive copy; get it from the Fire Marshal's Office or the city's permits page). Under the state table a business needs an LP-gas permit for storage and use of any size; Staunton's fee is $50 a year. Class II or IIIA combustible liquids above 25 gallons inside (60 outside) carry a $50 annual permit; Class I flammable liquids above 5 gallons inside (10 outside) are on the state table, with paints and solvents kept for maintenance for up to 30 days excepted. A propane tank also needs a building code gas permit and, for a buried or large tank, a storage tank permit ($200 per tank) from Building Services (glass_studio_building_mechanical). The Fire Marshal inspects before issuing the permit.
steps.deadline: Before the propane is delivered; the permit lapses if the activity does not start within six months
steps.fee: LP-gas $50.00 a year; Class II or IIIA liquid storage above 25 gallons inside $50.00 a year (City Code § 15.25.055, read on eCode360)
steps.quote: For the use and/or storage of LP Gas and Flammable/Combustible Liquids.

steps.step: Apply for the hazardous materials permit if oxygen or other gases exceed the table amounts, and for any other permit the Fire Marshal requires
steps.how: The city's Hazmat Storage Application covers storage of hazardous materials above the amounts in the local table (which lists gases by hazard class, as the state table does); the local fee is $50 a year. Oxygen is an oxidizing gas with a state permit threshold of 504 cubic feet at NTP (a few large cylinders), flammable gases 200 cubic feet, inert gases 6,000. If the office requires hot work, industrial oven, open flame or place of assembly permits, apply on the Fire Prevention Activity Application; the state code says applications are made on forms the fire official prescribes and that the fire official inspects or tests before issuing. Keep the compressed gas and hazmat quantities in the permit, since permits cover only what they say.
steps.deadline: Before the gases are stored or the activity begins
steps.fee: Hazardous materials $50.00 a year (City Code § 15.25.055, read on eCode360); other activity permits not priced on the schedule read
steps.quote: For the storage of hazardous materials.

steps.step: Pay the fees, pass the pre-issuance inspection and post the permits
steps.how: No fire code permit is issued until the fee in § 15.25.055 is paid (the state code lets the fire official allow delayed payment). The fire official makes the inspections or tests needed before issuing. Keep the issued permits on the premises and available to the fire official; permits are not transferable and lapse if the activity is not begun within six months or is abandoned for six months. Refunds on withdrawn applications are at the fire code official's discretion and capped at half the fee (§ 15.25.055(3), read on eCode360).
steps.deadline: Permits run for the period stated (the city's LP-gas and hazmat permits are annual)
steps.quote: Issued permits shall be kept on the premises designated therein at all times and shall be readily available for inspection by the fire official.

steps.step: Prepare for the yearly fire inspection
steps.who: Studio owner; Fire Marshal, Deputy Fire Marshal and Assistant Fire Marshals
steps.how: The office inspects commercial buildings, businesses and restaurants at least every year (frequency varies with staffing) and publishes a list of common fire code violations to review beforehand: exits and exit signs, extinguishers, electrical, storage clearances, address numbers and the like. For a hot shop expect attention to cylinder securing and separation of oxygen from fuel gases, clearances around the furnace, glory hole and kilns, combustible storage near heat, exhaust, and the occupant load and exits of the class and event rooms.
steps.fee: No fee stated for routine business inspections; § 15.25.057 (read on eCode360) sets fees only for licensure-related inspections
steps.quote: Business owners and managers are encouraged to review their safety practices and seek advice on current fire codes before our inspector arrives.

steps.step: If a sprinkler or alarm system goes out of service, notify the Fire Marshal and run a fire watch
steps.who: Studio owner; Fire Marshal's Office (nights and weekends 540.332.3884)
steps.how: Notify the fire department and the Fire Marshal immediately when a required fire protection system is out of service; the Fire Marshal may require evacuation or an approved fire watch until it is restored. The city publishes Fire Watch Duties, a Fire Watch Log and a Termination of Fire Watch form. Fire watch staff must have a way to call the fire department and do nothing but patrol for fire.
steps.deadline: Immediately when the system goes out of service
steps.quote: Where utilized, fire watches shall be provided with at least one approved means for notification of the fire department and their only duty shall be to perform constant patrols of the protected premises and keep watch for fires.

steps.step: For outdoor demonstrations, tents and events, get the event-side permits
steps.who: Studio owner or event organizer; Fire Marshal's Office; Building Official
steps.how: A tent or canopy over 400 and under 900 square feet needs a Fire Marshal tent permit ($25 per event); over 900 square feet or more than 50 people needs a building permit from the Building Official ($100 per tent) and inspection. Cooking is not allowed under a tent or canopy, open fires only in approved cooking appliances, and indoor flame-effects material needs a $100 per-event permit. A public glassblowing demonstration with open flame at a city event is the kind of activity to clear with the Fire Marshal on the Fire Prevention Activity Application; the city's special event application routes fireworks, live fire demonstrations and pyrotechnics to the Fire Marshal.
steps.deadline: Before the event; the city's special event application is due 60 days ahead
steps.fee: Tent 400 to 900 square feet $25.00 per event; indoor flame-effects material $100.00 per event (City Code § 15.25.055, read on eCode360); tent over 900 square feet building permit $100.00 per tent (§ 15.10.120, read)
steps.quote: Any tent larger than 900 square feet or accommodating more than 50 people requires a building permit from the Building Official and inspection. Tents larger than 400 square feet require an inspection by the Fire Marshal.

caveats: The Fire Permits & Inspections page is an Internet Archive copy of 18 August 2026; the three Fire Marshal application PDFs (LP gas, hazmat, fire prevention activity) have no archive copy and were not read.

Local law not quoted. City Code ch. 15.25 was read on eCode360 on 2026-10-19 and the fee amounts are reported as figures; eCode360's terms forbid reproducing its text. Confirm with the Fire Marshal's Office.

Staunton's fee table omits compressed gases, hot work, cutting and welding, industrial ovens, open flames and places of assembly, all of which the state Table 107.2 lets the fire official require. Whether the office requires those permits for oxygen cylinders, torches, a furnace and glory hole, or classes, and under what fee (the Fire Prevention Activity Application is the catch-all), is an open question only the office can settle.

Whether a glass furnace, glory hole or kiln is an industrial oven regulated by SFPC Chapter 30, and whether torch work is hot work or an open flame use, are classification questions for the Fire Marshal.
Which local board hears fire code appeals in Staunton (the Board of Building Code Appeals or another board) was not confirmed; § 27-98 provides for a local board and then the State Review Board.
The named Fire Marshal and other staff on the page are not recorded; the office line and role mailbox are.
